Guy Abargil, son of Dalia and David, was born on the 28th of Nisan 5736 (28 April 1976) at Kaplan Hospital in Rehovot. He is the brother of Eran, Smadar and Mordechai. As the eldest son and the first grandchild in the family, he was given special attention, and he returned the great love showered on him by giving it to everyone around him.

Guy grew up in Kiryat Malachi. Until the age of three he enjoyed the devoted care of his grandmother Dina. He then attended Hana's kindergarten, and in the early afternoons, when the kindergarten day ended, he would spend a few more hours with his grandmother until his parents returned from work.

Guy began his schooling at the Harel state-religious primary school in Kiryat Malachi, and even then his love of Torah and his love of people were evident. At the end of eighth grade he moved to Jerusalem, to the Kiryat Noar Technological High School, where he lived in the boarding school and studied electronics. He was an outstanding student. When his parents attended parent-teacher meetings they were gladdened by what the teachers and the educational advisor told them: "Guy is brilliant in his studies. He treats his teachers with respect and is loved by all his friends." Guy's friends described him as a unique personality. "The expression 'the salt of the earth' was invented especially for him," they said. His friend Meir Hadad emphasized: "An amazing man, head and shoulders above the rest. An outstanding personality, generous and wise in Torah."

At the end of twelfth grade, thanks to his high grades, Guy continued at Kiryat Noar in the military pre-service program and qualified as an electronics technician engineer.

On 11 July 1994 Guy enlisted in the Air Force. After basic training he was sent to the "Technical School," the Air Force Technological College in Haifa (the aviation technicians school), where he was trained as a ground control systems technician. Upon completing his studies he was posted to one of the Air Force bases in central Israel, where he served as a technician in the communications wing. In August 1999 he signed on as a career soldier.

During his service Guy married Odia and built a home in Israel. The couple settled in the town of Revava in Samaria and lovingly raised their two children, Michal and Nehorai. Guy was a devoted and loving husband and a perfect father. "The children and I were at the center of his world," Odia says. "He invested in the family above and beyond. He would come back from the base tired, and still he would play with the children and make them their supper." Guy also stood out for his devotion to his immediate family. He took a constant interest in the well-being of his parents and brother, looked after them, and even helped his sister financially, out of great humility asking her not to tell their parents.

After his move to Samaria, Guy was transferred to serve at the Air Force's air control unit at Hatzor, where he was in charge of communications and information systems. His friends and commanders speak of his professionalism, his high work ethic, and the order and precision that characterized his work, which became proverbial. These traits were combined with a pleasant and calm manner; his radiant smile never left his lips, he connected with everyone, he was a listening ear to many, and his inner calm drew others after him. "Not many people manage, without any special effort on their part, to change a person and give him the chance to become a better person... Guy was one of them," said Marak Alman, one of his unit comrades.

Guy was a modest and humble man, and his words and conduct were always free of hypocrisy and pretense. He was a man of truth whose inner self matched his outward appearance, and he always judged others favorably. His desire to give and to bestow was strong, and many soldiers were helped and supported by him. "Guy always wished well for everyone and never tried to gain anything at others' expense; he pursued his goals honestly, with a smile on his face and with innocence. I came to understand the concepts of good faith and love of one's fellow through his values and the graciousness of his manners," Marak continued, and Yisrael Zelka added: "Guy was an upright, humble and righteous person, one who invested in and helped anyone who asked for his help. He had a presence that cannot be described in words... With an angelic smile, he never raised his voice, and always spoke to each person 'at eye level.' He did his work above and beyond."

As a God-fearing Jew, Guy was careful to observe the commandments, the light and the severe alike. Faith and trust formed the foundation of his whole life; on various occasions, his friends recount, he would perceive the hand of Providence and give thanks for it... Guy made a point of setting fixed times for Torah study, helped establish a kollel in his town of Revava, and despite the late hours when he returned home, he kept up his daily study of the Mishnah. "A true tzaddik, a teacher and educator, a pure and good soul," said his friend Moshe Gozlan, with whom he studied.

On Shabbat Guy prayed at the Sephardi synagogue in Revava, where he served as a Torah reader and as prayer leader. Each Shabbat he arranged the rota of those reading from the Torah, and he encouraged young people to take part in the reading. The pleasantness of his prayer, his devotion and his intention would stir the heart and pierce the heavens... On joyous occasions of mitzvah, he would summon all his 248 limbs and 365 sinews and dance with his whole heart; he would take a Breslov kippah from his pocket, close his eyes, be carried away with enthusiasm, and at times weep from a feeling of exaltation...

At the base, Guy arranged a daily minyan for the afternoon prayer, and he used to teach the laws before the prayer. With his warm words and his very conduct he drew people closer to Torah and the commandments. Every Thursday Guy sent a Torah thought on the weekly portion through the Air Force's computerized mail network, and it was not for nothing that at the base they called him "Guy the Righteous."

Guy's good deeds were many, and his parents learned of most of them only after his death. Thus they found out that every month, without giving his name, Guy had been sending Rabbi Bahrav of Kiryat Malachi a check for one thousand shekels, which he asked to be given to the needy. The rabbi revealed the donor's identity only after Guy's death. The rabbi of Revava told the parents that two days before he fell, Guy had driven with him to Ariel, where some of the evacuees from the Gush Katif settlements had been taken. Guy, he related, helped distribute food, encouraged the evacuees and stayed with them the whole night until morning, even though he arrived late at the base as a result.

Guy's dream, his widow relates, was to complete his career service and retire, so that he could devote all his time to the study of Torah. But after six years of career service, Guy's life was cut short, leaving his family stunned, grieving and bleeding.

Guy fell in the performance of his duty on 20 Av 5765 (25 August 2005), in a traffic accident near Hizma, by the Kochav HaShachar junction. That day Guy was the duty officer of the base, and according to regulations he went out in an armored jeep with two security guards to escort a bus of soldiers who had finished their workday and were about to leave for the weekend. On their way back, two kilometers from the base, at a point where the road bends sharply, a Palestinian truck came at the jeep head-on, its driver speeding dangerously. The truck swerved out of its lane and crashed into the jeep with great force. Guy was killed on the spot. The two soldiers traveling with him were lightly to moderately wounded.

To the many journalists who covered the disaster, Guy's commander, Major Shuki Somech, said: "Guy was an upright and modest man; he never cut corners and never looked down on anyone. Religion was a central axis of his life, and yet he combined it with professionalism in his work. Thanks to his inner strength, and in his pleasant way, he managed to bring many people closer to tradition. He was also a model family man who always put his family first."

At Guy's grave, Nerya Shag, his colleague from the MIS (Management Information Systems) department, spoke words of farewell: "The Gemara says in tractate Shabbat: 'When one of the brothers dies, all the brothers will mourn; when one of the group dies, the whole group will mourn...' And we are mourning, Guy, not only because you were one of the group in the fullest sense of the word. We are also mourning because you were like one of the family to us, like brothers we were... You loved everyone, and you were loved by everyone, thanks to your character and your virtues. A modest person in the fullest sense of the word. Straight as a ruler, your head always on the work, with no wasted time. We trusted you one hundred percent. Every item and every detail was recorded and organized, and you always had an answer to every question... You gave every person the benefit of the doubt, and you loved every Jew. But above all you were a human being, a true friend, attentive, understanding and loving... We find parting difficult... Guy, be an advocate of integrity for your beloved family, and for the entire people of Israel. May your soul be bound up in the bond of life."

In the week after his fall, Meshael Shoker dedicated the daily halakhah lesson, on the subject of mourning, to the elevation of Guy's soul.

Guy's comrades in the unit parted from him with words they wrote in his memory. Itzik Borochov wrote: "Guy, my dear friend, I saw in you a good teacher and guide for life, who always wanted my well-being, and as your soldier you cared deeply about my interests... Although I knew you for only three months, I believe I was blessed with a friend and companion whom I will remember all my life."

Yossi Sasson wrote: "Guy, you are missing from me... I miss the nights of working together until the small hours, when I would be worn out and pull you into my room, and we would talk about ways to advance the department and about God's ways in the question of why 'the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper,' and how far the test of faith in trust in God extends. Every sentence in which you rebuked me about serving God or other matters was engraved in me, thanks to your pleasant personality, as criticism coming from the heart... May your rest be in Eden."

Yoel Ben Naim: "Guy said, 'I believe in the Creator of the world, who will stop and do everything for the good.' I hope that just as he cared for us here with the commandments, so he will watch over us from above and merit us with good deeds."

Shai Ohana: "... can you be proud of what you did here and of what you left behind? A family to be proud of and many good friends..."

Tzachi Ember wrote: "It was a pleasure for me to work with you, to pray with you, to serve with you, and to listen to the kind words that came out of your heart... At all times you were ready to help people, and you taught halakhah in the synagogue; with you it simply came from the heart... You loved everyone as if they were your brothers... I will remember you forever and try to take upon myself some of the good things you used to do."

Konstantin Fedosyev wrote: "I will always remember Guy with his smile and joy of life, for even in difficult and stressful moments there was a kind of happiness in his eyes..."

And Second Lieutenant Yehuda Sofer concluded: "... you always smiled, always were happy, always were there when help was needed... What a loss. I send many condolences to the family. With us too you were like a brother. We will never stop missing you..."

On the website of the town of Revava, a memorial page was dedicated to Guy, with his life story, photographs, a video in which he appears, and songs written in his memory by his friend Yogev Avraham.

One of Yogev Avraham's songs, "You Were a Friend to Me": "You were to me the wind / that made hard times pleasant / you were to me the quiet / for a heart that withstood the noise / you were to me the strength / when calm was lost within me / you were to me a friend / of smiles and love... // And within me remains a longing I'm used to, that breaks the heart / every time your absence / strikes me again in the face... / The memory, that grips hard and pinches the heart / at the entrance to your grave / conquered by my tears. // You were to me the echo / when difficulty became routine / you were to me the voice / that distinguishes good from evil / you were to me the compass / and pointed me to paths of joy / you were to me a friend / who encouraged me to succeed..."

Another song Yogev wrote is "Between the Mountains": "When I search for a familiar voice in the silence / I remember your voice calling my name / when I search for support and a helping hand / I imagine your figure standing beside me... // When I search for rest from the storm of my heart / perhaps I will find calm for my tears / when I search for the light that lay within me / I will find its radiance in front of me, my Nehorai... // Sometimes I want to unload the pain / and call out between the mountains your name, Guy, far away / for only so will you return / in the echo of my voice, which weakens / to the memory that beats within me and does not let go / for I will remember you with love."

Further poems Yogev wrote in memory of Guy appear on the website "Bama Hadasha" at http://stage.co.il/Stories/541848.

Guy was twenty-nine when he fell. He was laid to rest in the military section of the cemetery in Kiryat Malachi, with thousands of the town's residents accompanying him on his last journey.

Guy left behind a wife, a daughter aged three and a half and a son aged one year and four months, his parents, two brothers and a sister. After his death he was promoted to Master Sergeant. On his tombstone are engraved the words: "He feared God. A devoted family man."

May his memory be a blessing.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
